overview:
Kevala‑jñāna (Skt.; Prakrit: *kevala‑ñāṇa*) is the Jain term for omniscience — the complete, direct, and non-mediated knowledge attained by an *arihanta* who has destroyed all obscuring karmas. It is considered the highest state of cognition in Jain epistemology and marks the culmination of spiritual progress on the fourteen *guṇasthānas*. In both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, kevala‑jñāna is described as infinite, unobstructed, and simultaneous knowledge of all substances (*dravya*), their qualities (*guṇa*), and their modes (*paryāya*) across past, present, and future.

Jain philosophers classify knowledge into five types: *mati*, *śruta*, *avadhi*, *manaḥparyāya*, and *kevala*. Kevala‑jñāna stands apart because it is not acquired through sense organs, scriptures, or mental inference. Instead, it arises when the four *ghātiyā* karmas — *jñānāvaraṇīya* (knowledge‑obscuring), *darśanāvaraṇīya* (perception‑obscuring), *mohanīya* (deluding), and *antarāya* (obstructive) — are completely destroyed. The soul’s inherent luminosity becomes fully manifest.

In Digambara tradition, kevala‑jñāna is attained only after complete nudity and total renunciation, whereas Śvetāmbara texts allow kevala‑jñāna even for clothed ascetics. Both traditions agree that the omniscient being continues to live until the remaining *aghātiyā* karmas (body‑producing, lifespan, status, and feeling) are exhausted, after which the soul attains liberation (*mokṣa*).

Descriptions of kevala‑jñāna in canonical texts emphasize its non‑verbal, non‑discursive nature. The omniscient does not “think” in sequential steps; rather, knowledge is instantaneous and total. Commentarial literature often stresses that kevala‑jñāna is not merely vast knowledge but the complete removal of epistemic obstruction, revealing the soul’s natural state. Modern scholarship highlights its role in Jain soteriology as the definitive marker of spiritual perfection.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Kevala‑knowledge arises when the destructive karmas have been eliminated.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.1 is one of the most cited aphorisms defining the causal condition for omniscience. Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions accept this text, though they differ in interpretive details.

primary_sources.title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra (Śvetāmbara canon)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous canonical redaction
primary_sources.notes: A concise canonical statement affirming the omniscient’s total knowledge of substances and modes. The text belongs to the Śvetāmbara *aṅga* corpus.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama (Digambara canon)
primary_sources.author: Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali
primary_sources.translation: The culmination of knowledge is kevala.
primary_sources.notes: This early Digambara canonical text discusses the destruction of knowledge‑obscuring karma and the emergence of omniscience. Exact phrasing varies by manuscript tradition; the line here reflects a commonly cited recension.

misconceptions.myth: Kevala‑jñāna is a supernatural power that allows performing miracles.
misconceptions.reality: Primary texts describe kevala‑jñāna as perfect knowledge, not miraculous ability. Any extraordinary qualities arise from the destruction of karmas, not from magical intervention.

misconceptions.myth: Omniscience means constant verbal teaching of all knowledge.
misconceptions.reality: Canonical sources state that kevala‑jñāna is non‑verbal and instantaneous. The omniscient may teach through *divya‑dhvani* (Śvetāmbara) or remain silent (Digambara), but omniscience itself is not discursive speech.

misconceptions.myth: Only one Jain tradition accepts kevala‑jñāna.
misconceptions.reality: All major Jain traditions affirm kevala‑jñāna, though they differ in the conditions under which it is attained and how the omniscient communicates.
